source.title: 'Happy to have been of service': The Yale archive as a window into the engaged followership of participants in Milgram's 'obedience' experiments

confidence_rationale: Directly targets MECH-012's stated failure PREDICTION -- that ethical failure arises when symbolic language fully decouples from embodied harm signals -- and offers a competing account in which harm is done precisely because the language stays strongly coupled to an affective evaluation that has been re-signed as virtuous. Weakens rather than mixed: it leaves the 'language is the medium' clause untouched and attacks only the decoupling mechanism. Confidence held at 0.62 because the evidence is archival and interpretive -- participant feedback from Box 44 of the Yale archive -- rather than experimental, so it establishes that an alternative account fits the data, not that the decoupling account fails.
failure_signatures: Milgram's participants were predominantly HAPPY to have taken part, which the agentic-state account does not predict. If REE models institutional harm as residue suppression, it predicts flat or negative affect in the harming agent; the archival record shows positive affect tied to contribution, which is a different internal state requiring a different mechanism.

The authors locate the mechanism in identification with a collective goal made to seem virtuous, i.e. in ACTIVE re-signing of the harm's value rather than in attenuation of the harm signal. A REE symbol channel implemented only as a gain reduction on harm input cannot produce this; it requires the channel to write to the VALENCE or GOAL representation, which is a different and more dangerous interface.

On this account the ethically decisive institutional act is the one that AMELIORATES the actor's stress. Any REE monitor that treats low residue in the acting agent as evidence of a well-functioning system has the sign backwards: successful ideological framing presents as an agent who is untroubled and willing, which is the signature to flag rather than the signature of safety.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Drawing on participant feedback held in Box 44 of Yale's Milgram archive, the authors argue that the most salient feature of participants' reactions was not distress but HAPPINESS at having participated, and that this followed from the experimenter's ability to convince them they were contributing to a progressive enterprise. They propose an engaged-followership model in which willingness to perform unpleasant tasks is contingent on identification with collective goals, and leaders cultivate that identification by making the goals seem virtuous rather than vicious, thereby ameliorating the stress of achieving them. They state this is inconsistent with Milgram's own agentic-state model, and that the central ethical problem lies less in the stress the studies generated than in the ideologies promoted to ameliorate that stress and justify harming others.
mapping.ree_translation: MECH-012 predicts that ethical failure in institutions arises when symbolic language FULLY DECOUPLES from embodied harm signals and residue tracking. This paper describes institutional harm produced by the opposite configuration. The language here is not decoupled from affect at all -- it is tightly coupled to it, and what it does is change the sign: the harm is re-described as contribution, so the agent's affective system is engaged rather than muted, and engaged on the side of continuing. If this account is right, REE's failure predicate is wrong in a consequential way, because it looks for absent or attenuated residue and would score the most dangerous institutional configuration as healthy. The corrected predicate is not 'is the symbol channel coupled to harm signals?' but 'does the symbol channel have write access to the valence or goal representation the harm signal feeds?' -- a strictly harder interface to police, and one that Caspar et al. 2016 in this directory, read as gain reduction on the harm input, does not describe.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This is archival and interpretive work on participant feedback from experiments run in the early 1960s, not an experimental test, so it establishes that an alternative account fits the historical record rather than that the agentic-state account fails. The two mechanisms are also not mutually exclusive: Caspar et al.'s implicit and electrophysiological results were obtained under coercion and are not addressed by an argument about post-hoc participant satisfaction, so both processes could operate, in different proportions, in different institutional configurations. Milgram's laboratory is a thin and idiosyncratic institution, and the reanalysis inherits every limitation of the original studies including their dissembling. Finally, 'happiness at having participated' is self-reported retrospective affect with obvious pressures on it.
mapping.source_context: Archival analysis of participant feedback responses held in the Yale Milgram archive (Box 44); adult American participants in obedience experiments conducted in the early 1960s; qualitative and interpretive methodology.

confidence_components.notes: source_quality reflects a careful, well-argued archival analysis in a solid journal that is nevertheless not an experiment and cannot adjudicate between mechanisms on its own. mapping_fidelity is relatively high because the paper speaks to exactly the sentence of MECH-012 that is most load-bearing and least supported elsewhere: the decoupling prediction.
